canonical_title: Windows and Linux disagree on the lstat error code for 'path component is a file, not a directory' -- single-platform local empirical testing cannot substitute for real cross-platform CI
summary: During the S5-F-06 correction, a fail-closed ancestry-walk fix passed every local check on the Windows development machine (typecheck, lint, build, Prettier, 361/361 Fast Tests) but genuinely failed real GitHub Actions Linux CI (3 Fast Test failures). Empirical testing on Windows had shown that attempting to resolve a path through an ordinary file returns ENOENT; the same operation on Linux returns the POSIX-correct ENOTDIR. Both are fail-closed in effect (mapping to the same INVALID_OR_UNSAFE result), so this was a diagnostic-label and test-assertion defect, not a safety regression -- but it still could only be discovered by real Linux CI, not by more Windows testing.

claims.text: For the identical fixture (an ordinary file occupying a path position the code expects to be a directory), lstatSync on Windows empirically produced ENOENT while the same operation on the real Linux GitHub Actions runner produced ENOTDIR -- confirmed by reading the actual failing Linux CI job logs via `gh run view --job <id> --log`, not assumed from documentation.

evidence.locator: Section 10, 'Root cause of the CI failure': 'On this Windows machine, an ordinary file occupying an ancestor position empirically produces ENOENT... On Linux (the actual GitHub Actions runner), the POSIX-correct behavior for the identical fixture is ENOTDIR... Confirmed by reading the actual Linux CI job logs (gh run view --job <id> --log), not assumed.'

claims.text: The Linux-only failure was a narrower walk-up stopping one level too early and reporting the less specific METADATA_UNAVAILABLE status instead of INVALID_ANCESTRY, failing an exact-status test assertion -- both statuses fail-closed to the same INVALID_OR_UNSAFE reconciliation result, so no unsafe reconciliation outcome ever occurred on either platform.

evidence.locator: Section 10: 'This was not a safety regression: METADATA_UNAVAILABLE still maps to the same INVALID_OR_UNSAFE fail-closed reconciliation result; only the specific diagnostic label and one test's exact-substring assertion were affected.'

claims.text: The correction introduced a second, narrower helper (accepting both ENOENT and ENOTDIR) used only by the ancestry walk's own retry-up-one-level decision, while the pre-existing genuine-absence check at any single level remained ENOENT-only and completely unchanged in meaning -- deliberately avoiding a broad, unscoped redefinition of what counts as 'absent' anywhere in the system.

evidence.locator: Section 10, 'Correction': 'introduced a second, narrower helper, isUnresolvedPathError (ENOENT or ENOTDIR), used only by the walk-up loop's retry decision. isGenuineAbsenceError (the S5-F-05 function, ENOENT-only) is completely unchanged in meaning and in every other call site.'

conditions: Applies to any filesystem-boundary logic (existence checks, ancestry walks, permission probes) developed and empirically tested on one OS but deployed to or gated on another.

Most relevant when errno-level behavior differs across platforms in ways that are individually fail-closed-safe but not diagnostically equivalent, so tests asserting exact status/error strings can fail even though no unsafe outcome occurred.
anti_patterns: Treating a green local test run on one development platform as sufficient proof a filesystem-error-handling change is correct, without a real run on every platform the CI matrix and production target actually use.

Widening a narrowly-scoped error-code check (like a retry-vs-stop decision) into a broad redefinition of a differently-scoped check (like genuine-absence detection) just because both involve the same error code family -- the two concerns were kept deliberately separate here.
